clinicalPearls: Regarded as the juvenile or paediatric counterpart of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, sharing the same underlying genetics and behaviour
Typically presents as a slow-growing dermal and subcutaneous nodule or plaque in young children, with a male predominance and a predilection for the trunk and groin
Histology shows wavy spindle cells in a myxoid to collagenous stroma, distinctive branching pseudovascular (angiectoid) spaces, and scattered floret-like multinucleate giant cells lining those spaces
Diffusely CD34-positive, in keeping with its relationship to dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Driven by the COL1A1-PDGFB gene fusion, which places platelet-derived growth factor B under the control of the collagen gene promoter
Can occur combined with, and recur as, conventional dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, illustrating the continuum between the two
The pseudovascular spaces are not true vessels, which helps distinguish it from a vascular neoplasm
reference.pathophysiology: Giant cell fibroblastoma is a fibroblastic tumour driven by the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion, in which the platelet-derived growth factor B gene is placed under a constitutively active collagen promoter, producing autocrine PDGF receptor signalling that fuels proliferation. Because it shares this driver with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, the two are considered variants of one entity, and tumours can show hybrid or transitional features. The same molecular mechanism that sustains growth also makes the tumour susceptible, when advanced, to PDGF-receptor-directed tyrosine kinase inhibition, as used in unresectable dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.
additionalDifferentials: Vascular tumours, given the pseudovascular spaces
Kaposiform or other paediatric spindle cell lesions
additionalInvestigations: FISH or molecular testing for the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion
Endothelial markers to confirm the pseudovascular spaces are not true vessels
MRI or ultrasound to define the dermal and subcutaneous extent for planning excision
Margin assessment on the excision specimen to reduce recurrence risk
Review for any conventional dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans component
redFlags: Repeated local recurrence after inadequate excision
Transformation to or coexistence with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Any fibrosarcomatous change, which raises the risk of metastasis
reference.prognosis: Giant cell fibroblastoma is locally aggressive but does not usually metastasise, and wide local excision with clear margins is generally curative; incompletely excised tumours recur, sometimes as conventional dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, and only fibrosarcomatous transformation carries appreciable metastatic risk, so complete removal and follow-up are the mainstays.
pitfalls: Mistaking the pseudovascular spaces for a vascular tumour such as angiosarcoma
Failing to recognise the relationship to dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans and undertreating with narrow margins
Confusing it with benign dermatofibroma, leading to inadequate excision
Overlooking a coexisting or recurrent dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans component
Not using molecular testing when morphology is ambiguous in a paediatric spindle cell lesion
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Skin Tumours
management: Excise widely with clear margins, which is generally curative for this locally aggressive tumour
Use margin-controlled excision such as the Mohs technique where feasible to minimise recurrence
Reserve the PDGFR-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib for unresectable or advanced disease
Review histology for any dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans or fibrosarcomatous component
Maintain long-term surveillance for local recurrence, which may present as conventional dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Coordinate care across paediatric surgery, dermatology, pathology, and oncology
